strengths: The paper addresses a real bottleneck in HDR fusion: the lack of large-scale paired dynamic-scene HDR training data. A 24,000-sample synthetic HDR dataset, if released with sufficient metadata and tooling, would be a useful resource for this subfield.

The dataset construction is thoughtfully motivated, with attention to linear HDR rendering, EXR output, diverse motion categories, indoor/outdoor scenes, lighting conditions, camera shake, and exposure augmentation.

The empirical section evaluates multiple modern HDR fusion architectures, including CNN and transformer baselines, and reports improvements across SCT and Challenge123 using standard PSNR/SSIM variants and HDR-VDP2.
The paper includes useful ablations separating the effect of S2R-HDR pretraining, fine-tuning, the two adapter branches, uncertainty scaling, and teacher-student test-time adaptation.
Qualitative examples support the central intuition that the synthetic dataset helps in large-motion and high-dynamic-range cases where small real datasets are limited.
weaknesses: The novelty of S2R-Adapter is limited. The adapter design, low/high-rank branches, uncertainty-based scaling, and mean-teacher test-time adaptation are heavily borrowed from prior domain adaptation/TTA work, with relatively modest task-specific technical innovation.

The main state-of-the-art comparisons are not fully fair: the proposed models benefit from pretraining on 24,000 synthetic samples plus adaptation, while many baselines are trained directly on small real datasets. The paper does not consistently compare against equally scaled pretraining, generic synthetic pretraining, or stronger adaptation baselines applied to the same architectures.

Evaluation on real data is narrow and small: SCT has 36 test samples and Challenge123 has 27. This makes the SOTA claims fragile, especially without statistical significance, per-scene breakdowns, robustness analysis, or evaluation on more real-world HDR/mobile/video benchmarks.

The dataset quality analysis is suggestive but not fully convincing. Metrics such as t-SNE visualization and simple HDR/diversity statistics do not establish physical realism, camera pipeline fidelity, sensor noise realism, or whether synthetic artifacts bias the learned models.

The paper claims dataset and code availability, but the URL is blank in the manuscript. For a dataset-centered submission, missing release details, licensing, asset provenance, rendering scripts, and reproducibility documentation are serious concerns.

The test-time adaptation protocol needs more scrutiny. The teacher model is updated across test samples, so performance may depend on test ordering and implicit target-set adaptation; the paper does not analyze order sensitivity, failure cases, computational overhead, or risks of degradation under distribution shifts.

Ablations are helpful but incomplete. The paper does not compare against simpler alternatives such as full fine-tuning with regularization, LoRA-only adapters, domain randomization, synthetic-to-real image translation, or training with matched-size subsets to isolate scale versus rendering fidelity.

Several claims are overstated, such as “first large-scale high-quality synthetic dataset” and broad real-world generalization, given limited external validation and lack of released materials. The writing also contains some terminology and grammar issues that reduce clarity.

strengths: The paper targets an important bottleneck in HDR fusion: the lack of large paired training data for dynamic HDR scenes, especially with large motion and extreme illumination.
A 24,000-sample synthetic HDR dataset, if released with the claimed EXR data and generation pipeline, could be useful to the HDR reconstruction community.
The paper evaluates the dataset across multiple recent HDR fusion architectures, including CNN and transformer baselines, and reports consistent gains after synthetic pretraining plus adaptation.
The method includes several relevant ablations on dataset source, adapter branches, test-time adaptation components, and forgetting, which helps isolate some effects of the proposed ingredients.
weaknesses: The central empirical comparison is not sufficiently fair. In Table 2, the proposed models benefit from large-scale synthetic pretraining plus real-data adaptation, while many competing methods are compared as directly trained on small real datasets. The paper does not convincingly show that the gains come from the proposed dataset/adapter rather than simply from substantially more training data or additional fine-tuning.

The adapter contribution appears incremental and under-positioned relative to existing low-rank/high-rank adapter and test-time adaptation methods such as ViDA and mean-teacher consistency. The paper largely repackages known mechanisms for HDR fusion without a strong technical novelty argument.

The dataset quality claims are weakly supported. The diversity analysis relies on handcrafted summary metrics and t-SNE visualizations, which do not establish photorealism, sensor realism, correct HDR statistics, or real-world transfer. There is no user study, no systematic realism validation, and limited analysis of synthetic artifacts.

Reproducibility is a major concern. The abstract says 'Dataset and code will be available at' but provides no link. The rendering pipeline, UE5 assets, scene construction, camera/exposure simulation, licensing, and train/test generation details are not specified enough to reproduce or audit the dataset.

The real-world evaluation is narrow: primarily SCT and Challenge123, both very small. The strongest claims about state-of-the-art real-world HDR reconstruction and generalization are therefore overclaimed relative to the evidence.

The test-time adaptation setting is under-evaluated. The paper compares mostly against models trained on other datasets rather than strong source-free/test-time adaptation baselines, and it does not analyze per-sample runtime, stability, failure cases, or sensitivity to augmentation/uncertainty calibration.

Some reported results are internally awkward or insufficiently discussed. For example, S2R-HDR pretraining performs much worse than real training on SCT in PSNR-mu before adaptation, while performing very well on Challenge123; this asymmetric behavior raises questions about domain bias and dataset coverage.

The paper lacks important practical details and ethical/resource discussion, including compute cost for rendering and training, licensing of UE assets/humans/animals/vehicles, potential release restrictions, and environmental cost of generating a large synthetic dataset.

Presentation quality is uneven, with grammatical issues, vague claims such as 'high quality' and 'superior visual quality,' and several places where method descriptions are too high-level to support careful reproduction.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear bottleneck in dynamic HDR fusion: the scarcity of large, diverse, paired HDR training data. A 24,000-sample rendered HDR dataset with controllable motion, lighting, camera shake, and EXR ground truth is a meaningful resource for this subarea.

The experimental results are consistently positive across multiple recent HDR fusion backbones, including CNN- and transformer-based models, suggesting that the dataset contribution is not tied to a single architecture.

The paper evaluates both supervised adaptation to real HDR datasets and a more challenging unlabeled/test-time adaptation setting. This makes the practical motivation stronger than a dataset-only submission.

The ablation studies are useful: they separately examine the dataset, adapter branches, scale factors, teacher-student TTA framework, and forgetting behavior. These experiments support the main story that synthetic pretraining plus adaptation improves real-data generalization.
The visual examples and quantitative gains on SCT and Challenge123 are compelling, especially for ghosting reduction, motion occlusion, and highlight recovery.
weaknesses: The main methodological novelty of S2R-Adapter is moderate. The two-branch low-/high-rank adapter design, uncertainty-based scaling, and teacher-student TTA are largely adaptations of existing ideas, and the paper could better clarify what is fundamentally new beyond applying these components to HDR fusion.

The evaluation is still limited by the small size and narrow scope of available real benchmarks. Most claims about real-world generalization are based on SCT and Challenge123, with additional appendix results but no broad stress testing across more cameras, sensors, exposure patterns, noise levels, or real lighting extremes.

Some comparisons may be somewhat imbalanced: the proposed models benefit from large-scale synthetic pretraining plus adaptation, while many baselines are trained only on small real datasets. Stronger baselines using comparable pretraining, generic rendered data, domain randomization, LoRA/adapters, full fine-tuning, or existing TTA methods would make the gains more conclusive.

The paper claims dataset and code availability but the manuscript appears to leave the release link blank. For a dataset-centered submission, missing concrete access, licensing, generation scripts, and reproducibility details are a significant weakness.

The dataset quality analysis relies on hand-selected HDR diversity metrics and t-SNE plots, which are helpful but not fully convincing as evidence of realism or coverage. A more direct human study, sensor-model validation, or real/synthetic domain-gap quantification would strengthen the contribution.

Several implementation details are underspecified, including exact training schedules, optimization hyperparameters, rendering asset provenance/licensing, camera/exposure sampling distributions, and how synthetic LDR inputs are matched to real camera pipelines. These details matter for reproducibility and for judging whether the dataset will be broadly reusable.

The writing is understandable but has recurring grammar and terminology issues, and some claims are overstated relative to the evidence, such as broad claims of state-of-the-art real-world HDR reconstruction from evaluations on a small set of benchmarks.

strengths: Introduces a practically valuable large-scale synthetic HDR fusion dataset with 24,000 HDR frames, substantially larger and more diverse than commonly used real HDR fusion datasets.
The paper addresses an important bottleneck in HDR fusion: scarcity of ground-truth dynamic-scene HDR data, especially with large motion and extreme illumination.

Evaluation is fairly broad for the subarea, covering SCT, Challenge123, Kalantari, Real-HDRV, and HDR video reconstruction settings, with multiple architectures including transformer- and CNN-based baselines.
Results consistently show that pretraining on S2R-HDR followed by adaptation or fine-tuning improves cross-dataset generalization and downstream HDR fusion quality.
The S2R-Adapter is simple, plug-and-play, and evaluated in both supervised adaptation and unlabeled test-time adaptation settings, with useful ablations of its branches and uncertainty scaling.
weaknesses: The adapter itself is only moderately novel, largely combining existing LoRA/adapter and mean-teacher test-time adaptation ideas; the main contribution is the dataset rather than a major algorithmic advance.
Reproducibility is a concern: the manuscript leaves the dataset/code URL blank, and the generation pipeline depends partly on purchased UE5 assets, making full independent reproduction difficult.

The evaluation sometimes conflates gains from much larger synthetic pretraining with gains from the proposed adapter; while ablations help, stronger comparisons to alternative adaptation methods and synthetic-data training schemes would be valuable.

The claimed state-of-the-art comparison is not fully airtight because several baselines appear trained under different data/adaptation regimes rather than all being given the same synthetic pretraining and adaptation budget.

The test-time adaptation method adds per-sample optimization and augmentation overhead, and its stability, sensitivity to uncertainty scaling, and behavior under long test streams are not deeply analyzed.

Dataset quality/diversity metrics are useful but somewhat indirect; more human perceptual studies or camera-realism validation would strengthen the case that the synthetic data closes the relevant real-world domain gaps.
Some writing and presentation issues remain, including typos, inconsistent table labels, duplicated/incorrect figure captions in the appendix, and an unfinished availability statement.

strengths: The paper addresses a real bottleneck in HDR fusion: the lack of large, diverse paired training data for dynamic scenes, especially scenes with large motion and extreme lighting.

A 24,000-frame UE5-rendered HDR dataset with EXR data and auxiliary modalities such as flow/depth/normals could be useful to the community if actually released with clear licensing and reproducible generation details.

The experiments cover several HDR fusion backbones and multiple target datasets, and the reported numbers suggest that synthetic pretraining followed by adaptation can improve performance over training on small real datasets alone.
weaknesses: The main experimental comparisons are not convincing enough for a top-tier venue. The proposed models use an additional 24k synthetic dataset plus adaptation, while many baselines are trained only on small real datasets, so the reported gains conflate data scale, pretraining, fine-tuning, and the adapter mechanism.

The adapter contribution is technically incremental: it is essentially a low/high-rank residual adapter with learned or uncertainty-scaled coefficients, plus a standard mean-teacher test-time adaptation framework. The paper does not provide enough analysis to establish that this design is novel or necessary beyond standard LoRA/adapters, fine-tuning, or existing TTA methods.

The dataset quality claims rely heavily on hand-picked visual examples, simple HDR/diversity statistics, and t-SNE plots. These do not establish photorealism, sensor realism, domain fidelity, or whether the synthetic ground truth matches real capture physics well enough for HDR fusion.

Reproducibility is weak. The manuscript leaves the dataset/code URL blank, uses purchased UE5 assets and Photomatix, and does not provide enough detail on scene assets, rendering settings, training budgets, optimization schedules, or licensing to reproduce the dataset or results.

The supervised adaptation setting is arguably unfair: the proposed method adapts on the target training set after synthetic pretraining, but the baselines are not all given comparable synthetic pretraining, adapter tuning, or test-time adaptation under matched compute and data conditions.

The test-time adaptation protocol is underspecified and potentially problematic. It is unclear whether the model is reset between images/datasets, how ordering affects results, whether adaptation uses all test samples transductively, and how the uncertainty value is normalized before being used as a scale factor.

Several ablations are too narrow. The paper does not sufficiently compare against stronger alternatives such as full fine-tuning with matched regularization, LoRA-only adapters, domain randomization, adversarial adaptation, self-supervised HDR methods under the same protocol, or synthetic pretraining on other rendered datasets with the same adaptation recipe.

Some reported improvements are modest or inconsistent, especially for the adapter alone, while the paper repeatedly makes strong claims about state-of-the-art performance and generalization. The evidence does not fully support the breadth of these claims.

The writing and presentation contain notable issues, including repeated tables/figures, typo-level errors, an empty availability statement, and somewhat overstated interpretations of t-SNE visualizations and diversity metrics.

strengths: The paper tackles an important bottleneck in HDR fusion: the lack of large, diverse paired training data for dynamic high dynamic range scenes. A 24,000-sample UE5-rendered HDR dataset with auxiliary modalities is a meaningful resource contribution for this area.

The empirical evidence is fairly broad for an HDR fusion paper: results are reported on SCT, Challenge123, Kalantari, Real-HDRV, Sen/Tursun no-reference settings, and an HDR video reconstruction extension. The improvements are consistent across multiple backbones, including SCTNet and SAFNet.

The ablations are useful. The paper separately studies the effect of S2R-HDR pretraining, supervised adaptation, test-time adaptation, the two adapter branches, uncertainty-based scaling, and knowledge forgetting.

The method is practically motivated. A plug-and-play adapter for CNN and Transformer layers, with no added inference overhead after reparameterization for supervised adaptation, is appealing for existing HDR fusion systems.
The dataset analysis is stronger than a purely qualitative dataset paper: the authors quantify HDR extent, intra-frame diversity, dynamic range, motion/scene distributions, and visualize domain gaps.
weaknesses: The main technical novelty of S2R-Adapter is moderate. The two-branch low-rank/high-rank adapter and uncertainty-scaled test-time adaptation are closely inspired by existing adapter/TTA literature, and the paper does not compare against enough direct domain adaptation baselines to isolate whether the proposed adapter is better than standard LoRA/adapters, full fine-tuning with regularization, DANN-style adaptation, source-free TTA, or domain randomization.

The evaluation sometimes conflates dataset scale and adaptation method. Many comparisons pit models trained on small real datasets against models pretrained on a 24,000-sample synthetic dataset and then adapted; this is a valid practical setting, but the causal attribution to dataset quality versus sheer data volume, scene selection, training budget, and adaptation is not fully disentangled.

Reproducibility is weaker than claimed: the main text says code and dataset are available, but the URL is blank in the manuscript. The dataset also relies partly on purchased UE5 scene assets, and the exact licensing, redistributability, and reconstruction of those assets are not fully clarified.

The real-world evaluation is still limited by small target test sets, e.g. SCT and Challenge123 contain only dozens of test samples. The paper reports strong gains, but statistical uncertainty, split sensitivity, and possible overfitting to common HDR benchmarks are not addressed.

The dataset realism validation could be stronger. The t-SNE and seven handcrafted HDR statistics are useful but do not fully establish that rendered sensor characteristics, noise, saturation, camera response, demosaicing, and real motion artifacts match physical capture pipelines.

The test-time adaptation setup needs more scrutiny. It processes each sample once but uses multiple augmentations and model updates at inference; runtime is reported, but memory cost, stability across sample order, failure modes under low-quality pseudo-labels, and comparison to simpler test-time augmentation without weight updates are limited.

Some presentation and polish issues remain, including typos such as 'Domain Adaption', duplicated or mislabeled figures around optical flow distribution, table typos like PNSR/DHR-VDP2, and incomplete resource links. These do not invalidate the work, but they reduce confidence in readiness.
